description: I'm an early-stage founder, filmmaker and national-level exhibitor at a government-recognised science expo. I'm building a platform that brings fragmented reports of public-infrastructure damage together so municipalities can identify and solve city problems. I enjoy Unreal Engine game development, web systems and visual storytelling, and use DaVinci Resolve. Join X Factor to build boldly. We're seeking teammates in coding, game design, 3D/animation, space science, UI/UX and data.
summary:
Lunar Outpost Mission Trainer is a free 3D browser game that makes children aged 7–12 the commander of a four-person outpost near Shackleton Crater at the Moon’s south pole. Over ten mission days the player chooses cargo, places the solar array, hunts for water ice, and brings the crew through a real solar flare and a two-day particle storm before handing over a working base.

It answers the “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge by making NASA data something children play, not read. Real solar flares from NASA’s DONKI space-weather database drive the storms: tap the peak of the 11 May 2024 X5.8 flare to win extra warning time, or choose one of this month’s real flares to face. A gold “This is real” banner explains each cause and effect in one line, and practice data is always labelled as practice.

It matters because the Artemis generation is in primary school now. The game teaches the real trade-offs of living off Earth: the water you drink is also your oxygen, shielding the solar array from a storm costs power, and every repair outside costs radiation dose. It plays in 10 or 25 minutes, in one file that opens with a double-click: no install, no account, no personal data collected, and it works offline in a classroom.
details:
Lunar Outpost Mission Trainer is a 3D browser game for ages 7–12. The player commands four astronauts at an outpost near Shackleton Crater for ten mission days: choose the cargo, place the solar array, find water ice, survive a real solar flare and a two-day particle storm, then hand over a working base. It plays as 8 chapters of 3–5 minutes (about 25 minutes) or a 10-minute Quick mission.

Each astronaut has a job: power, rover and repairs, greenhouse, or crew health. The player drags an astronaut onto a task, runs the shift, and reads a report in child-friendly language that says what happened and why. Eight short mini-games, such as landing cargo by crane and finding an oxygen leak, turn engineering jobs into play. Pip, a scout robot, gives tips and can be switched off.

NASA data is the game mechanic:

Flare Spotter: the Sun’s brightness meter replays a real flare from NASA’s DONKI database (28 Oct 2021 X1.0, 11 May 2024 X5.8 or 11 Nov 2025 X5.1). Tapping at the peak earns extra warning time.

Sun Deck: real flares from the last 30 days appear as cards. A stronger flare means a harder storm and a higher score.

Experiment Lab: the player predicts the result of a real NASA Open Science Data Repository study and earns a perk.

Water to air: the oxygen rule uses NASA’s life-support baseline of 0.84 kg of oxygen per person per day.

Mission Control briefing: the two-peak storm is modelled on the August 1972 solar storms between Apollo 16 and 17.

Benefits

Children learn the real trade-offs of living off Earth. Drinking water is also the crew’s oxygen. Shielding the solar array from a storm costs power. Every repair outside costs radiation exposure. A “Data Detective” question after each data moment checks understanding, and class codes give a whole classroom the same mission to compare.

Intended impact

The Artemis generation is in primary school now. We want any teacher or parent to run a 10-minute space mission on any school computer, with no install, no account and no internet, and for children to finish knowing that space weather is real, measurable and survivable with good planning.

Tools, languages and software

JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS; a custom WebGL renderer; a Node.js script that packs the whole game into one HTML file; Python scripts that convert the 3D astronaut model and lunar texture; the Web Speech and Web Audio APIs for read-aloud and sound; the NASA Open APIs (DONKI); and Playwright for automated browser playthroughs. Code and in-game text were generated with AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic).

Creativity

Most educational games show data on a card. Here the data decides the game: the real flare’s timing sets the player’s warning, and its strength sets the storm.

Factors we considered

Honesty: every source is marked real, saved or practice in the game. A gold “This is real” banner marks NASA data, and practice data is never shown as NASA data.

Accessibility: read-aloud on every card, captions, text size, an easy-read font, a colour-blind mode, a calm mode, and mouse, touch or keyboard control.

Access and privacy: one double-clickable file that works offline; no accounts, and progress is saved only in the browser.

Reliability: 40 automated rule and data tests, plus automated playthroughs at desktop and phone sizes.
